newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: DEFAULTED ZAIRE DEBT: A NEW PUNT FOR INVESTORS.
newsitem.headline: DEFAULTED ZAIRE DEBT: A NEW PUNT FOR INVESTORS.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's military victory in former Zaire has spurred interest in its defaulted commercial debt as investors bet on his ability eventually to overhaul the shattered economy, analysts said on Tuesday.
The old debt of what is now the Democratic Republic of Congo is currently indicated at 12.00/15.00 cents in the dollar.

That does not signal much confidence in the chance of loans being repaid, but it is up from the 11.00/13.00 seen before the fall of Kinshasa 10 days ago and 10.00/11.00 last month, according to South African broker Investec Securities.

"Now that Kabila is in there I am sure he will be looking for fresh sources of income and one of his first priorities must be a consolidation of defaulted debt and a rescheduling," said Investec's John Clemmow.
"There is no way Kabila is not going to try and come back to the debt market and there is no way he is going to be allowed to do so unless he deals with the existing debt."

Analysts estimate Zaire's foreign debt at $14 billion, most of it owed to commercial banks. The country defaulted on repayments in 1992 and since then has paid little interest or principal on existing loans.

Buying up distressed former Zaire debt is not an investment for widows and orphans. But to specialist "vulture funds", who scour the world for undervalued paper, and other yield-hungry investors, it is starting to look attractive.

The hope is that Kabila's new government will be able to untap some of the vast copper and other mineral wealth in Zaire, and at the same time adopt orthodox economic policies to stabilise the economy.

In any case, most observers say economic prospects and hence the chances of old debts being repaid can hardly be worse under the new government than under the collapsed regime of former president Mobutu Sese Seko, who ruled for 32 years.

At the same time new Finance Minister Mawampanga Mwana Nanga is seen as good news. Educated in the United States, where he lived for over 10 years, Mawampanga is the seen as the brains behind the alliance's broadly free-market economic policies.

Dealing with the billions of dollars worth of old debt is a prerequisite for country to get new credits -- something which economists see as essential to rebuild collapsed infrastructure, including the worst roads in Africa.

"It's going to be difficult for Kabila to do much with the economy as long as there is this major debt overhang. The pressure will be on to resolve the debt issue," said an economist with one major South African bank.

Peter Worthington, economist at JP Morgan in London, said investors could have to wait a year or more before seeing any resolution to the old debt issue, but for those prepared to sit it out there might be big rewards.
"People are betting on the possibility that Kabila will put something in place to sort out the debt problem...the upside is potentially very large," he said.
"This country does have huge capacity to generate foreign exchange if it can appropriately exploit its mineral resources."
